questions.stitle: Scenario 1 - Hospital network with competing clinical options
questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the EA team of a not-for-profit hospital network that is standardizing patient records across twelve hospitals. The network uses the TOGAF Standard; the Chief Medical Information Officer sponsors the EA program. A Statement of Architecture Work is approved and Phase A is under way. Two seemingly competing options have emerged: (1) a single new electronic patient record optimized for the network, and (2) a federated model that keeps each hospital's existing record but reconciles data through a shared layer. Clinicians, hospital administrators, and the privacy office each have strong and partly conflicting concerns about safety, workflow disruption, cost, and patient privacy.
questions.q: You have been asked how you would select the best option for the program. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Identify the key stakeholders and their concerns, assess the impact of the two options across the architecture domains working with the other domain architects and clinical SMEs, assess the security and privacy concerns in the Business, Application, and Information Systems Architectures, and facilitate the stakeholders selecting their preferred option by trading off concerns, changes, costs, and benefits.
o.B: Identify the stakeholders and the SMEs most involved in information management, assess the impact of the two options on the existing hospital systems, collaborate with the SMEs on the privacy concerns for each option, then select the best option yourself and propose it as the way forward.
o.C: Identify the program's stakeholders and clinical leads, work with SMEs to assess the two options using the architecture trade-off method, list the advantages and disadvantages of each, select the best option, integrate it into the Implementation and Migration Plan, explain it to the stakeholders, and oversee its implementation.
o.D: Identify the new record system's stakeholders and their concerns, assess the impact of the two options on the existing hospital IT systems, collaborate with SMEs, assess the privacy concerns in the Application and Information Systems Architectures, and work with the stakeholders to trade off concerns, changes, costs, and benefits so they select their preferred option.

rat.A: Best (5). You assess the options across all domains and against multiple concerns so the stakeholders can make a well-informed decision. Security and privacy span uncertainty and defense across every domain, each option reflects one domain's perspective, and only stakeholders decide the relative merit of conflicting concerns.
rat.D: Second (3). It narrows the scope to the record system's stakeholders rather than all program stakeholders and limits the assessment to the hospital IT systems, ignoring possible Business Architecture impact and part of the security and privacy picture.
rat.B: Third (1). Good EA centers on the stakeholder making an informed decision where interests compete; this is damaged by the architect selecting a best option on unstated criteria and then pushing it through. Only stakeholders can approve the Target Architecture.
rat.C: Distractor (0). You are not advising stakeholders across their competing concerns; you are selling a chosen option and stepping into implementation oversight.

questions.stitle: Scenario 2 - Postal operator adding parcel lockers
questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the EA team of a national postal operator that is launching a network of automated parcel lockers to complement home delivery. The operator uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. An Architecture Vision is approved and there is high-level agreement across domains. A Baseline Description of the current Business Architecture exists, including a business capability map and value stream descriptions for the delivery business. A packaged locker-management solution is available but aligns poorly with the current routing and customer-notification systems. The team leader asks how you would identify the changes required in the Business Architecture.

o.A: Model the current state of the business using capability, value stream, organization mapping, and information mapping, focus on improving the existing capabilities and value streams because baseline descriptions exist, and document where the business needs to change.
o.B: Determine where the current business (organizational design, processes, capabilities) does not support the locker network, describe the options for change and their costs to stakeholders so they can decide, identify where trade-off decisions are needed, and work with the stakeholders to resolve them.
o.C: Review and update the current architecture descriptions to reflect the present state, draw up target descriptions defining new value streams and a capability map for the locker business, map value stream stages to capabilities, and perform a capability gap analysis.
o.D: Request the packaged locker solution's documentation, define the changes needed to align it with the routing and notification systems, sequence them into an Architecture Roadmap, and get references from other operators to confirm the vendor can meet the dates and service levels.

rat.B: Best (5). Phase B focuses on the business: find where it does not support the change, describe the options and their costs, and work with stakeholders on the trade-offs, engaging them in the decision.
rat.C: Second (3). Updating descriptions and building target value streams and a capability map with a gap analysis is a valid Phase B technique, but it is more model-focused and does not yet require committing to the packaged solution.
rat.A: Third (1). Modeling only, with no stakeholder engagement, and it wrongly assumes the focus should be improving existing capabilities and value streams just because baselines exist.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Not Business Architecture; it is implicit architecture with the architect acting as SME and implementer, jumping to a vendor solution.

questions.scenario: You are a Senior Architect in the EA team of an airline extending its loyalty program with personalized offers. The airline uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. A review of the Business Architecture with key stakeholders identified where current value streams and information flows produce inconsistent offers and slow campaign launches. The stakeholder communities' core motivations were confirmed as faster campaign launch, a consistent personalized experience, and driving down the sustained cost of maintaining duplicated loyalty data stores. The team leader notes that stakeholders agree the experience can improve but the information flows consume heavy IT resources that drive cost up.
questions.q: The team leader asks what you need to establish to address the motivation to drive down sustained cost. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Determine where the current Application Architecture and Data Architecture create the information-flow problems, identify the changes needed to fix the flows, look for incremental changes that improve the personalized experience, identify the one-time work and its impact on reducing sustainment cost, and check with stakeholders whether the experience improvements are worth the one-time and ongoing cost.
o.B: Produce application and data models of the current state, develop a Target Architecture model that enables faster launches and lower cost, create views describing the changes in those terms, and identify the gaps between current and target to build roadmap components.
o.C: Determine where the Application and Data Architecture fail to support campaign launch and the personalized experience and drive cost up, focus on the logical application and logical data components, identify the changes that improve launch and cost, determine the work, and obtain stakeholder priorities on the application development, data structures, and interfaces.
o.D: Identify where the Application Architecture (the information system services and logical application components) fails to support campaign launch and personalization and drives cost up, determine the changes to the information flows that enable faster launch and lower cost, and identify stakeholder priorities for the enhanced capability, improved value stream, and improved information flow.

rat.A: Best (5). All changes carry value and cost; stakeholders accept a Target Architecture on the cost of change and expected outcome, not a data model. Phase C discovers where the current Application and Data Architecture cause the deficiency, then assesses the direct and sustainment cost of the change with stakeholders, feeding Phase E and Phase F.
rat.D: Second (3). It identifies stakeholder priorities and changes to information flows, but does not explicitly assess the one-time and ongoing costs of the change with stakeholders. This leaves cost-of-change information needed by Phases E and F incomplete.
rat.C: Third (1). No analysis of the information flows known to cause the deficiency; it focuses on logical components without a real Target Architecture and asks stakeholders for priorities on implementation detail.
rat.B: Distractor (0). Jumps to modeling and optimizing the Application and Data Architecture with no linkage to the value-stream and information-flow deficiencies from the Business Architecture.

questions.stitle: Scenario 4 - Energy trader consolidating data platforms
questions.scenario: You are an Architect in the EA team of an energy trading firm consolidating several analytics platforms onto a common high-performance technology stack. The firm uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. The Business, Data, and Application Architectures are approved by stakeholders and their platform requirements are understood. A Technology Portfolio Catalog and current infrastructure standards exist. Stakeholders are concerned about latency, resilience, and the total cost of the new stack. The team leader asks how you would develop the Technology Architecture.

o.A: Baseline the current technology using the Technology Portfolio Catalog and standards, define the target platform needed to support the approved application and data components, perform a gap analysis against the standards, and work with stakeholders to trade off the latency, resilience, and cost implications of the candidate technology options.
o.B: Produce a Platform Decomposition Diagram and Environments and Locations Diagram for the target platform, identify the technology gaps against the baseline, record the candidate roadmap components, and refine the diagrams as products are procured.
o.C: Document the target platform decomposition in detail, list the technology gaps, and hand them to the infrastructure team to select products, deferring the latency and cost questions to Implementation Governance.
o.D: Select the platform the largest trading desk already prefers, procure it to accelerate delivery, and document the resulting environment as the Technology Architecture so implementation can start immediately.

rat.A: Best (5). Phase D develops the Technology Architecture that supports the application and data components: baseline with the catalog and standards, define the target, run a gap analysis, and engage stakeholders on the latency, resilience, and cost trade-offs. The architect assesses options so stakeholders can decide.
rat.B: Second (3). The platform and environment diagrams plus gap analysis and roadmap components are correct Phase D technique, but they do not surface the latency, resilience, and cost trade-offs to stakeholders for decision.
rat.C: Third (1). It produces the target and gaps but hands product selection to the infrastructure team and defers the stakeholders' concerns to a later phase, which is too late.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Jumps to procuring a specific product on a desk's preference with no Technology Architecture, gap analysis, or trade-off, ignoring the stated concerns.

questions.stitle: Scenario 5 - Established bank facing challenger competition
questions.scenario: You are an Enterprise Architect recently recruited to a bank that has grown by acquisition, leaving duplicate systems, inconsistent data, and heavy reliance on in-house integrations. The bank uses the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. Customers are switching to challenger banks with lower fees, faster service, and an always-available digital experience. The CIO decided the core infrastructure and services must be rationalized and must accommodate constant technology and business change. An Architecture Vision is approved and a set of domain architectures with gaps has been approved by stakeholders. The team has identified the work needed to realize the changes.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend the best approach to move forward. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Have the EA team review existing projects and deliverables against the gap analysis per domain, have each domain architect produce projects to close its gaps and revise existing project scope where needed, consolidate the work per domain into the Implementation and Migration Plan, and document the timeline in the Architecture Roadmap.
o.B: Implement the domain architectures and revise the scope of all in-flight projects to align, create new IT projects for the requirements not addressed, ensure all projects expose data and functionality through defined service interfaces, and publish this as the Implementation and Migration Plan.
o.C: Identify the dependencies among the proposed changes and organize them into work packages that address the gaps, assess value, effort, and risk for each change and work package against stakeholder priorities, identify a series of Transition Architectures ensuring measurable business value is delivered incrementally, and document the work packages and Transition Architectures in the Architecture Roadmap.
o.D: Have stakeholders provide input on what must be done to implement the domain architectures, roll the result into an IT portfolio plan and a series of projects, and form a comprehensive Target Architecture including detailed technology choices for the next five years.

rat.C: Best (5). Phase E: consider dependencies, organize changes into work packages, assess value, effort, and risk against stakeholder priorities, and use Transition Architectures for incremental value that addresses the need to absorb constant technology and business change, documented in the Architecture Roadmap.
rat.A: Second (3). Names the Plan and Roadmap accurately but rolls up work domain by domain rather than as consolidated capability management and does not directly use Transition Architectures.
rat.D: Third (1). Considers stakeholder priorities but ends in fixed five-year technology choices, negating the incremental value of Transition Architectures.
rat.B: Distractor (0). Does not follow Phase E guidance and jumps to a technical solution (service interfaces) without considering transition.

questions.stitle: Scenario 6 - Merged insurers with resistant business lines
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at an insurer formed by merging two mid-sized companies. The operating model is unified and an EA project runs as part of the integration. The company uses the TOGAF ADM; the newly appointed CIO sponsors the EA program. An outline Implementation and Migration Plan is approved and detailed planning is under way. Others outside the EA team will fund, build, support, and use what is put in place. The business lines have resisted new products and processes. The CIO wants risk reduction, timely progress, and an incremental rollout with key value delivered in each increment.
questions.q: You have been asked to describe how the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan should be created. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Have the EA team's domain architects define a series of Transition Architectures to deliver value incrementally, create a prioritized activity list documented in the Implementation and Migration Plan with a detailed schedule in the Architecture Roadmap, and circulate these to the business lines and Executive Board so they are ready to fund the work.
o.B: Finalize the plan with the domain architects and submit it to the Architecture Board for approval, incorporating its feedback; the plan includes a prioritized project list, approximate cost, estimated effort, schedule, and a sequenced timeline usable as the Architecture Roadmap.
o.C: Have Business Planning, Portfolio Management, and Operations Management join the EA team in migration planning, create detailed resource estimates and business value for all deliverables, plan a series of Transition Architectures that consider stakeholder priorities, finalize the Implementation and Migration Plan, and complete the architecture development cycle once deliverables are done.
o.D: Have the business-line Project Managers use the Phase E Implementation and Migration Strategy to build project plans on scope, budget, and time, define business value project by project, select the highest-value projects, and request funding from the Architecture Board.

rat.C: Best (5). Phase F emphasizes collaborative planning with stakeholders inside and outside the organization (Business Planning, Portfolio, Operations Management with the EA team), resource estimates and business value for deliverables, and Transition Architectures based on stakeholder priorities.
rat.A: Second (3). It uses Transition Architectures but is EA-team-centric and merely circulates the result, lacking the close collaborative planning across the wider stakeholder groups.
rat.B: Third (1). Incomplete; it misses the collaborative planning with stakeholders inside and outside the organization that Phase F requires.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Hands strategic migration planning to Project Managers; TOGAF's intent is that the EA gives projects detailed guidance so they focus on operational, not strategic, issues.

questions.stitle: Scenario 7 - Logistics firm deploying a COTS route optimizer
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at a logistics firm with a mature EA practice using the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. After consulting key stakeholders, the CIO has decided to deploy a COTS route-optimization package quickly and within budget. The package needs a message broker that is not on the current infrastructure standards list. The Architecture Board noted the non-standard component and the need to protect performance and security KPIs. The CIO has approved the roadmap projects and appointed a project manager, and stresses that performance and security KPIs must be maintained or exceeded and the project must stay within budget.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend a plan to implement the CIO's direction. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Prepare a detailed risk assessment and impact analysis of the non-standard broker, hand the deliverables and deployment dates to the implementation team, obtain CIO approval before implementation starts, test the solution just before deployment to confirm performance, and archive the artifacts in the repository when done.
o.B: Accept the direction, add the message broker as an additional organizational standard in the Standards Library (noting the training and skills needed to support it), work with the implementation team to draw up an Architecture Contract, emphasize compliance reviews and performance and security testing during implementation, agree SLAs and dates with the business, and collect reusable artifacts afterward.
o.C: Ask the vendor to modify the broker to meet current standards, build a prototype to explore options, obtain the internal development leads' approval, hand a schedule-focused project plan to the project manager, and review performance after go-live.
o.D: Eliminate the non-standard broker, create a revised plan and Architecture Contract to build a standards-compliant replacement in-house, tell the CIO this is lower cost long term, take the budget impact to the finance committee, and chair frequent project meetings to monitor compliance and schedule.

rat.B: Best (5). All within Phase G: accept the decision already made with stakeholders, add the new standard to the Standards Library (noting training and skills), draw up an Architecture Contract with the implementation team, emphasize compliance reviews and performance and security testing during implementation, agree SLAs and dates with the business, and collect reusable artifacts afterward.
rat.C: Second (3). The vendor change and prototype cost time and budget, which the scenario forbids; the project plan is the project manager's job; and reviewing performance only after go-live is too late.
rat.A: Third (1). Follows the direction but focuses on risk over co-existence, just hands over deliverables and dates with no negotiation on service levels, and tests too late (after the solution is built).
rat.D: Distractor (0). Reverses a decision the CIO already made with stakeholders, makes unsubstantiated cost claims, involves the finance committee irrelevantly, and has the architect chairing project meetings.

questions.stitle: Scenario 8 - Software firm with a new data-residency law
questions.scenario: You are Lead Architect at a software company whose target architecture has been implemented and is in production, governed under the TOGAF Standard; the CIO sponsors the EA program. A new data-residency law has just been enacted that requires customer data for one large market to remain in-country. A Change Request has been raised describing the deviation from the current architecture. The Architecture Board has asked you how to handle it. The change is significant and could affect the Business, Data, Application, and Technology Architectures.
questions.q: You have been asked to recommend how to handle the Change Request. Which is the best answer?

o.A: Treat the Change Request as an input to Architecture Change Management, assess its impact through a requirements impact assessment (which requirements, stakeholder priority, which ADM phases to revisit, and recommendations), and on that basis decide whether a simple change update suffices or a new ADM cycle is warranted, referring the recommendation to the Architecture Board and stakeholders.
o.B: Immediately open a new full ADM cycle from the Preliminary Phase to redesign the architecture for the new law, since any legal change of this size clearly requires starting over.
o.C: Assess the impact of the Change Request across the domains and, if the change is contained, apply it as an incremental update to the architecture through change management without launching a new cycle, escalating to a new cycle only if the impact analysis shows it is warranted.
o.D: Log the Change Request in the repository and defer any action until the next scheduled architecture review, since the current architecture is already in production and stable.

rat.A: Best (5). The Change Request is the key input to Phase H. TOGAF requires assessing its impact (requirements affected, stakeholder priority, ADM phases to revisit, recommendations) and then deciding between a change update and a new ADM cycle, with the recommendation going to the board and stakeholders who hold the decision rights.
rat.C: Second (3). It correctly assesses impact and distinguishes an incremental update from a new cycle, but it does not frame the formal requirements impact assessment or the referral of the recommendation to the board and stakeholders.
rat.B: Third (1). Starting a full new cycle may be the outcome, but jumping there without an impact assessment skips the Phase H decision step and may be disproportionate.
rat.D: Distractor (0). Deferring action on a live legal-compliance Change Request ignores the purpose of Phase H, which is to manage change to the architecture as it arises.
